title: Illness and prayer
hookLine: pray Ardas and take the medicine; Guru Har Rai kept a herb garden
tomorrow: Harjit has slept in a hospital chair for days. who looks after him?

lines: ARDAS ALL THE WAY TO THE ER.
DO THE PATH, OR SIGN THE FORM?
cards: Both, as it turns out. Harjit drives, Simran in the back seat holding Bebe's hand, and Bebe says Ardas under her breath the whole way to the ER. The scan shows a broken hip.
The surgeon wants to operate in the morning. By ten that night the family group chat has two camps. One auntie posts a line from the Sukhmani: the Name is the medicine for every illness.
Do the path, she writes, trust the Guru. Harjit types back: and sign the form. Simran watches both messages sit there, side by side.

teach.h: SUKHMANI: THE NAME IS THE MEDICINE.
teach.b: Let each side speak at its best. The auntie first. Her line is real, from the Sukhmani on Ang 274, in paraphrase: the Name is the medicine for every illness.
Fear, panic, the feeling of being alone in a hospital bed: Naam reaches those, and trust in hukam, God's order, keeps a family from falling apart while the body heals.
Some readers hear the line as about the deepest sickness of all, haumai, the I, I, I, that no surgeon can cut out. Now Harjit's side. Sikh memory of the Gurus includes medicine.
Tradition says Guru Har Rai kept a garden of healing herbs and gave medicine to people who came to him for it, and stories say he sent remedies even to a Mughal prince.
Ardas itself is asking for help, and the help can arrive in scrubs. Refusing a doctor isn't Sikh teaching. In Bebe's room, the argument ends the way Bebe likes arguments to end: she's in charge.
Ardas tonight, she says, and the surgery at eight.
Then she asks Simran for her gutka and a pen for the form.
Pray and heal, in that order, and also at the same time.

how: Sikh families facing illness say Ardas for the sick, sometimes hold a Sukhmani path or Akhand Path, and also follow medical care; gurdwaras include the sick in the congregation's Ardas.

o: saying Ardas and taking the medicine, side by side
a promise that prayer heals any illness at once
a rule to fast until a sick person recovers

games.q: two sides, one room — tap the pairs.
p: the Name is the medicine for every illness

s: Sikh teaching says to refuse doctors and rely only on prayer
tradition remembers Guru Har Rai's garden of healing herbs, and Bebe signs the form after Ardas.
some readers hear 'the Name is the medicine' as about haumai too
the deepest sickness, the I, I, I, is one no surgeon can reach.
Ardas is a prayer of asking
it asks for help, and in a hospital the help can arrive in scrubs.

games.q: you're on Harjit's side. what is the strongest case for the auntie's view?
o: Naam reaches what surgery can't: fear, loneliness, haumai, a family falling apart.
old people just prefer prayer because they distrust hospitals.
doctors can't be trusted, so prayer is the only safe choice.
games.why: her best case isn't anti-doctor: it's that illness is more than a bone, and the Name tends the parts no scan shows. Bebe keeps both.

practice: Rest one hand flat on your chest and the other on your belly, and sit upright. Feel the body that carries you, rising and falling, for the whole sit.
Hold in mind someone who is sick, in your Ardas if you pray, and let each steady breath go their way.

wordCard.voice: Illness and prayer. Saying Ardas and taking the medicine, the way the Gurus' own herb garden and the Sukhmani sit side by side.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: aukhadh, medicine; in the Sukhmani, the Name is the medicine for every illness.

carryVoice: For the road: pray and heal, the Ardas and the doctor in one room. That's today.

sources.ref: Ang 274, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan (sarab rog kaa aukhadh naam), paraphrased
